concept.name: Z-score
concept.definition: The number of standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean of its distribution, obtained by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. Z-scores standardize values from different distributions onto a common scale.
concept.intuition: It converts any measurement into 'how many sigmas from average' - a -2 day means a move twice the typical size in the down direction, whatever the asset's units.
concept.mechanics: Compute z = (x - mu)/sigma using the population parameters, or (x - x_bar)/s with sample statistics. Under a normal model the z-score maps directly to tail probabilities via the standard normal CDF (z = +/-1, +/-2, +/-3 contain about 68%, 95%, 99.7% of mass).
concept.formula: z = (x - mu) / sigma, where x is the value, mu the mean, and sigma the standard deviation; sample form z = (x - x_bar)/s.
concept.failure_modes: Tail probabilities read off a z-score assume approximate normality; for fat-tailed returns a -5-sigma event is vastly more common than the normal table implies, so z-scores understate tail risk. They are also unreliable when the mean and standard deviation are themselves unstable or estimated from few observations.
concept.misconceptions: A z-score is not itself a probability, and |z| > 2 is a rough rule of thumb for 'far from average', not a rigorous outlier test - OpenStax notes it is approximate, not a rigid rule. Also, z-scoring does not make non-normal data normal.
concept.example: With mean daily return 0.04% and sigma 1%, a day returning -2.96% has z = (-2.96 - 0.04)/1 = -3.0, i.e., three standard deviations below the mean.
